subject: maths
title: Year 5 Equivalent Fractions and Mixed Numbers
seo_title: Year 5 Equivalent Fractions and Mixed Numbers Worksheets: Improper Fractions, Comparing and Ordering (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Compare and order fractions whose denominators are all multiples of the same number; identify, name and write equivalent fractions of a given fraction, represented visually, including tenths and hundredths; recognise mixed numbers and improper fractions and convert from one form to the other and write mathematical statements > 1 as a mixed number [for example, 2/5 + 4/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5].
meta_desc: Free Year 5 maths worksheets on equivalent fractions and mixed numbers for the National Curriculum: fraction walls, tenths and hundredths, missing numerators and denominators, improper fractions, comparing and ordering fractions and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and the bottom by the same number.
key_sub: 3/4 = 9/12 (× 3). 3/10 = 30/100. 11/4 = 2 3/4, because 4 goes into 11 twice with 3 left over.
body_html:
Equivalent fractions

Equivalent fractions show the same amount. To find one, multiply (or divide) the numerator and the denominator by the same number. The parts get smaller, but there are more of them.

Example

34 = ?12

4 × 3 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 3 too: 3 × 3 = 9.

Answer: 912

Tenths and hundredths

In a hundred square, each column is 1 tenth and each small square is 1 hundredth. So 1 tenth = 10 hundredths.

Improper fractions and mixed numbers

An improper fraction such as 114 is greater than 1. A mixed number such as 2 34 shows the same amount as wholes and a fraction.

Example

Write 175 as a mixed number.

5 goes into 17 three times (15), with 2 left over.

Answer: 3 25

Example

Write 2 35 as an improper fraction.

2 wholes = 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths: 10 + 3 = 13.

Answer: 135

When an answer is more than 1, write it as a mixed number: 25 + 45 = 65 = 1 15.

Comparing and ordering

When one denominator is a multiple of the other, change one fraction so they have the same denominator. Then compare the numerators.

Example

Order 34, 58 and 12 from smallest to largest.

Use eighths: 34 = 68, 58, 12 = 48.

Answer: 12, 58, 34

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Multiplying only the numerator: 23 = 43Multiply both: 23 = 46
Adding the same number to the top and bottom: 23 = 45Multiply or divide, never add: 23 = 46
2 35 = 65 or 235Wholes × denominator, then add the numerator: 2 × 5 + 3 = 13, so 135
Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction: 18 > 14A bigger denominator means smaller parts: 18 < 14

faq.q: What fractions do Year 5 children learn?
faq.a: Year 5 pupils find equivalent fractions (including tenths and hundredths), convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers, and compare and order fractions whose denominators are multiples of the same number. They also add and subtract fractions and multiply them by whole numbers.

faq.q: How do you teach equivalent fractions in Year 5?
faq.a: Start with bars, a fraction wall and a hundred square so children see that the amount stays the same. Then show the rule: multiply or divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number, for example 3/4 = 9/12.

faq.q: How do you change an improper fraction to a mixed number?
faq.a: Divide the numerator by the denominator. The answer is the number of wholes and the remainder is the new numerator, so 17/5 = 3 2/5. To go back, multiply the wholes by the denominator and add the numerator: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.

faq.q: How do you compare fractions with different denominators?
faq.a: If one denominator is a multiple of the other, change one fraction so both have the same denominator, then compare the numerators. For 2/3 and 7/12, 2/3 = 8/12, so 2/3 is greater.

items.q:
The bars are the same size and show the same amount.
13 = ?6
items.e: The bottom bar has 6 equal parts, so each third of the top bar is split into 2 parts. 1 third becomes 1 × 2 = 2 sixths. So 13 = 26.

items.q:
The bars are the same size and show the same amount.
34 = ?8
items.e: The bottom bar has 8 equal parts, so each quarter of the top bar is split into 2 parts. 3 quarters become 3 × 2 = 6 eighths. So 34 = 68.

items.q:
The bars are the same size and show the same amount.
25 = ?10
items.e: The bottom bar has 10 equal parts, so each fifth of the top bar is split into 2 parts. 2 fifths become 2 × 2 = 4 tenths. So 25 = 410.

items.q:
The bars are the same size and show the same amount.
23 = ?12
items.e: The bottom bar has 12 equal parts, so each third of the top bar is split into 4 parts. 2 thirds become 2 × 4 = 8 twelfths. So 23 = 812.

items.q:
The bars are the same size and show the same amount.
34 = ?12
items.e: The bottom bar has 12 equal parts, so each quarter of the top bar is split into 3 parts. 3 quarters become 3 × 3 = 9 twelfths. So 34 = 912.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 23 is shaded. How many twelfths are equal to 23?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each third is the same as 4 twelfths, so 2 thirds line up with 2 × 4 = 8 twelfths. So 23 = 812.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 34 is shaded. How many eighths are equal to 34?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each quarter is the same as 2 eighths, so 3 quarters line up with 3 × 2 = 6 eighths. So 34 = 68.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 35 is shaded. How many tenths are equal to 35?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each fifth is the same as 2 tenths, so 3 fifths line up with 3 × 2 = 6 tenths. So 35 = 610.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 56 is shaded. How many twelfths are equal to 56?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each sixth is the same as 2 twelfths, so 5 sixths line up with 5 × 2 = 10 twelfths. So 56 = 1012.

items.q:
Each column is 110 of the square. 3 columns are shaded.
310 = ?100
items.e: Each column has 10 small squares, so each tenth = 10 hundredths. 3 tenths = 3 × 10 = 30 hundredths. So 310 = 30100.

items.q:
70 small squares are shaded.
70100 = ?10
items.e: 70 hundredths fill 7 whole columns. Each column is a tenth, so 70100 = 710. (Divide 70 and 100 by 10.)

items.q: Which fraction is equal to the shaded part?
items.e: 90 of the 100 small squares are shaded: 90100. That is 9 full columns, so it is also 910. 90100 is the answer. 9100 is only 9 small squares, and 10100 is the part that is not shaded.

items.q: What fraction of the square is shaded?
items.e: 50 of 100 squares = 50100 = 510. Half of the square is shaded, so 50100 = 12.

items.q: 40100 is shaded. Which fraction is not equal to the shaded part?
items.e: 4 columns are shaded: 40100 = 410 = 2050 = 25 (2 columns out of every 5). 4100 would be only 4 small squares.

items.q: 912 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 3. Which equal fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 4 groups and 3 of them are shaded, so 912 = 34. This is the same as dividing 9 and 12 by 3.

items.q: 410 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 2. Which equal fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 5 groups and 2 of them are shaded, so 410 = 25. This is the same as dividing 4 and 10 by 2.

items.q: 68 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 2. Which equal fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 4 groups and 3 of them are shaded, so 68 = 34. This is the same as dividing 6 and 8 by 2.

items.q: 1015 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 5. Which equal fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 3 groups and 2 of them are shaded, so 1015 = 23. This is the same as dividing 10 and 15 by 5.

items.q: 812 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 4. Which equal fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 3 groups and 2 of them are shaded, so 812 = 23. This is the same as dividing 8 and 12 by 4.

items.q: 1216 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 4. Which equal fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 4 groups and 3 of them are shaded, so 1216 = 34. This is the same as dividing 12 and 16 by 4.

sets.title: Find the missing numerator or denominator

items.q: 23 = ?12
items.e: Look at the denominators: 3 × 4 = 12. Multiply the numerator by 4 too: 2 × 4 = 8. So 23 = 812.

items.q: 35 = ?20
items.e: Look at the denominators: 5 × 4 = 20. Multiply the numerator by 4 too: 3 × 4 = 12. So 35 = 1220.

items.q: 58 = ?24
items.e: Look at the denominators: 8 × 3 = 24. Multiply the numerator by 3 too: 5 × 3 = 15. So 58 = 1524.

items.q: 47 = ?28
items.e: Look at the denominators: 7 × 4 = 28. Multiply the numerator by 4 too: 4 × 4 = 16. So 47 = 1628.

items.q: 56 = ?30
items.e: Look at the denominators: 6 × 5 = 30. Multiply the numerator by 5 too: 5 × 5 = 25. So 56 = 2530.

items.q: 710 = ?100
items.e: Look at the denominators: 10 × 10 = 100. Multiply the numerator by 10 too: 7 × 10 = 70. So 710 = 70100.

items.q: 14 = ?100
items.e: Look at the denominators: 4 × 25 = 100. Multiply the numerator by 25 too: 1 × 25 = 25. So 14 = 25100.

items.q: 25 = ?100
items.e: Look at the denominators: 5 × 20 = 100. Multiply the numerator by 20 too: 2 × 20 = 40. So 25 = 40100.

items.q: 34 = 15?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 3 × 5 = 15. Multiply the denominator by 5 too: 4 × 5 = 20. So 34 = 1520.

items.q: 25 = 8?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 2 × 4 = 8. Multiply the denominator by 4 too: 5 × 4 = 20. So 25 = 820.

items.q: 56 = 25?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 5 × 5 = 25. Multiply the denominator by 5 too: 6 × 5 = 30. So 56 = 2530.

items.q: 79 = 21?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 7 × 3 = 21. Multiply the denominator by 3 too: 9 × 3 = 27. So 79 = 2127.

items.q: 1824 = ?4
items.e: 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so divide the numerator by 6 too: 18 ÷ 6 = 3. So 1824 = 34.

items.q: 40100 = ?10
items.e: 100 ÷ 10 = 10, so divide the numerator by 10 too: 40 ÷ 10 = 4. So 40100 = 410.

items.q: 1520 = 3?
items.e: 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so divide the denominator by 5 too: 20 ÷ 5 = 4. So 1520 = 34. Taking 12 from both (to get 38) changes the value.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 35?
items.e: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number: 3 × 4 = 12 and 5 × 4 = 20. So 35 = 1220. Multiplying only one number changes the value.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 49?
items.e: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number: 4 × 2 = 8 and 9 × 2 = 18. So 49 = 818. Multiplying only one number changes the value.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 710?
items.e: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number: 7 × 10 = 70 and 10 × 10 = 100. So 710 = 70100. Multiplying only one number changes the value.

items.q: Which fraction is not equivalent to 23?
items.e: 45 is not equal to 23: 2 was added to the numerator and the denominator of 23. Adding the same number changes the value. The others are equivalent, because both numbers were multiplied by the same number.

items.q: Which fraction is not equivalent to 34?
items.e: 56 is not equal to 34: 2 was added to the numerator and the denominator of 34. Adding the same number changes the value. The others are equivalent, because both numbers were multiplied by the same number.

items.q: Each bar is 1 whole. 114 are shaded. Write this as a mixed number.
items.e: Each bar is 1 whole. 2 bars are full and 3 more parts are shaded in the last bar. So 114 = 2 34.

items.q: Each bar is 1 whole. 83 are shaded. Write this as a mixed number.
items.e: Each bar is 1 whole. 2 bars are full and 2 more parts are shaded in the last bar. So 83 = 2 23.

items.q: Which letter shows 74?
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 equal parts, so each mark is 14. 74 = 1 34: go to 1, then 3 more marks. That is letter B.

items.q: Which letter shows 135?
items.e: Each whole is split into 5 equal parts, so each mark is 15. 135 = 2 35: go to 2, then 3 more marks. That is letter C.

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed number.
items.e: Each whole is split into 3 equal parts, so each mark is 13. The arrow is 2 marks after 2. So it shows 2 23 (= 83).

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed number.
items.e: Each whole is split into 6 equal parts, so each mark is 16. The arrow is 5 marks after 1. So it shows 1 56 (= 116).

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed number.
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 equal parts, so each mark is 14. The arrow is 1 mark after 2. So it shows 2 14 (= 94).

items.q: Write 135 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 5s go into 13? 2 × 5 = 10, so there are 2 wholes. 13 − 10 = 3 are left over. So 135 = 2 35.

items.q: Write 174 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 4s go into 17? 4 × 4 = 16, so there are 4 wholes. 17 − 16 = 1 is left over. So 174 = 4 14.

items.q: Write 196 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 6s go into 19? 3 × 6 = 18, so there are 3 wholes. 19 − 18 = 1 is left over. So 196 = 3 16.

items.q: Write 2310 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 10s go into 23? 2 × 10 = 20, so there are 2 wholes. 23 − 20 = 3 are left over. So 2310 = 2 310.

items.q: Write 298 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 8s go into 29? 3 × 8 = 24, so there are 3 wholes. 29 − 24 = 5 are left over. So 298 = 3 58.

items.q: Write 227 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 7s go into 22? 3 × 7 = 21, so there are 3 wholes. 22 − 21 = 1 is left over. So 227 = 3 17.

items.q: Write 2 35 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 55, so 2 wholes are 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add the 3: 10 + 3 = 13. So 2 35 = 135.

items.q: Write 3 14 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 44, so 3 wholes are 3 × 4 = 12 quarters. Add the 1: 12 + 1 = 13. So 3 14 = 134.

items.q: Write 4 23 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 33, so 4 wholes are 4 × 3 = 12 thirds. Add the 2: 12 + 2 = 14. So 4 23 = 143.

items.q: Write 1 710 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 1010, so 1 whole is 1 × 10 = 10 tenths. Add the 7: 10 + 7 = 17. So 1 710 = 1710.

items.q: Write 5 38 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 88, so 5 wholes are 5 × 8 = 40 eighths. Add the 3: 40 + 3 = 43. So 5 38 = 438.

items.q:
25 + 45 = 65 = ?
Write the answer as a mixed number.
items.e: 25 + 45 = 65 (add the numerators, keep the fifths). 55 make 1 whole and 1 fifth is left over. So the answer is 1 15.

items.q:
34 + 34 + 34 = ?
Write the answer as a mixed number.
items.e: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9, so the total is 94. 4 × 2 = 8, so that is 2 wholes and 1 quarter left over: 2 14. Do not add the denominators.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Which is greater: 23 or 712?
items.e: 12 is a multiple of 3, so use twelfths: 23 = 812 and 712. 8 > 7, so 23 is greater.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Which is greater: 58 or 34?
items.e: 8 is a multiple of 4, so use eighths: 58 and 34 = 68. 6 > 5, so 34 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 35 or 710?
items.e: 10 is a multiple of 5, so use tenths: 35 = 610 and 710. 7 > 6, so 710 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 49 or 13?
items.e: 9 is a multiple of 3, so use ninths: 49 and 13 = 39. 4 > 3, so 49 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 56 or 1112?
items.e: 12 is a multiple of 6, so use twelfths: 56 = 1012 and 1112. 11 > 10, so 1112 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 34 or 68?
items.e: 8 is a multiple of 4, so use eighths: 34 = 68 and 68. The numerators are the same, so they are equal.

items.q: Which is greater: 12 or 512?
items.e: 12 is a multiple of 2, so use twelfths: 12 = 612 and 512. 6 > 5, so 12 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 710 or 1320?
items.e: 20 is a multiple of 10, so use twentieths: 710 = 1420 and 1320. 14 > 13, so 710 is greater.

items.q: Which fraction is the greatest?
items.e: Write them all with the denominator 16: 34 = 1216, 58 = 1016, 1116, 12 = 816. The greatest is 1216, so the answer is 34.

items.q: Which fraction is the smallest?
items.e: Write them all with the denominator 12: 23 = 812, 56 = 1012, 712, 512. The smallest is 512, so the answer is 512.

items.q: Which fraction is the greatest?
items.e: Write them all with the denominator 20: 35 = 1220, 710 = 1420, 1320, 25 = 820. The greatest is 1420, so the answer is 710.

items.q: Which fraction is the smallest?
items.e: Write them all with the denominator 18: 49 = 818, 13 = 618, 518, 29 = 418. The smallest is 418, so the answer is 29.

1720, 45, 710

items.q: Which fraction is between 12 and 34?
items.e: In eighths: 12 = 48 and 34 = 68. 58 is between them. 78 and 45 are more than 34, and 38 is less than 12.

items.q: Which fraction is between 13 and 23?
items.e: In twelfths: 13 = 412 and 23 = 812. 512 is between them. 112 is less than 13, and 34 = 912 and 56 = 1012 are more than 23.

items.q: Oliver eats 38 of a pizza. Amelia eats 12 of a pizza of the same size. Who eats more?
items.e: Use eighths: 12 = 48. 4 eighths is more than 3 eighths, so Amelia eats more.

items.q: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Harry eats 34 of it. How many slices does he eat?
items.e: 4 × 2 = 8, so 34 = 68. Harry eats 6 slices.

items.q: Isla has a 1 m ribbon. She cuts off 310 m. How many centimetres is that?
items.e: 1 m = 100 cm. 310 = 30100, so she cuts off 30 cm.

items.q: In a hundred square, Jack colours 45 squares red. What fraction is red, in tenths and hundredths?
c: 4100 + 5100
410 + 5100
510 + 4100
items.e: 45 hundredths = 4 full columns (4 tenths) and 5 more squares (5 hundredths). So 45100 = 410 + 5100.

items.q: Poppy uses 23 of a bag of flour. Arjun uses 56 of the same size bag. Who uses more flour?
items.e: Use sixths: 23 = 46. 5 sixths is more than 4 sixths, so Arjun uses more.

items.q: Ava runs 114 km. Write this distance as a mixed number.
items.e: 4 × 2 = 8 and 11 − 8 = 3. So 114 km = 2 34 km.

items.q: Each jug holds 13 litre of water. Noah pours out 7 jugs. How much water is that, as a mixed number?
items.e: 7 jugs of 13 litre = 73 litres. 3 thirds make 1 litre, so 6 thirds make 2 litres, with 1 third left over: 2 13 litres.

items.q: Aisha says, “18 is greater than 14, because 8 is greater than 4.” Is she right?
c: No. 18 is less than 14
Yes. Eighths are bigger than quarters
items.e: A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into more, smaller parts. 14 = 28, which is more than 18. So 18 is less than 14.

items.q: George says 2 35 = 65. What is the correct improper fraction?
items.e: George multiplied 2 × 3. Instead, 2 wholes = 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths: 10 + 3 = 13. So 2 35 = 135.

items.q: Lily changed 23 into an equivalent fraction and wrote 45. What did she do wrong?
c: She multiplied only the numerator by 2
She added 2 to the top and the bottom
items.e: 2 + 2 = 4 and 3 + 2 = 5. Adding changes the value. Multiply both numbers by 2 instead: 23 = 46.

items.q: Four children measure their ribbons. Leo: 34 m. Grace: 78 m. Kai: 58 m. Zara: 12 m. Who has the longest ribbon?
items.e: Use eighths: 34 = 68, 78, 58, 12 = 48. The longest is Grace’s ribbon.

items.q: A cake is cut into 12 equal slices. Ruby eats 3 slices. What fraction of the cake is that, in its simplest form?
items.e: 3 out of 12 slices = 312. Divide both numbers by 3: 312 = 14.

items.q: Mohammed cycles 2 14 km to school. Write this distance as an improper fraction.
items.e: 2 km = 2 × 4 = 8 quarters. Add 1 quarter: 8 + 1 = 9. So 2 14 km = 94 km.

items.q: A bottle holds 710 litre of squash. A jug holds 35 litre. Which holds more?
items.e: Use tenths: 35 = 610. 7 tenths is more than 6 tenths, so the bottle holds more.

items.q: At a party, children eat 19 slices of pizza. Each pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. How many pizzas do they eat?
items.e: 6 slices make 1 pizza. 3 × 6 = 18, and 19 − 18 = 1 slice is left. So 196 = 3 16 pizzas.

items.q: Charlie walks 56 km to the park and 56 km back home. He writes 56 + 56 = 106 km. Write the total as a mixed number.
items.e: 6 sixths make 1 km. 10 − 6 = 4 sixths are left over. So 106 km = 1 46 km (which is also 1 23 km).

items.q: Three classes each have the same size pot of paint. Class 5A uses 34 of theirs, Class 5B uses 916 and Class 5C uses 58. Which class uses the least paint?
items.e: Use sixteenths: 34 = 1216, 916, 58 = 1016. The smallest is 916, so Class 5B uses the least. 16 is the biggest denominator, but that does not make it the biggest fraction.

items.q: Evie has 3 25 bars of chocolate. Each bar has 5 equal pieces. How many pieces does she have?
items.e: 3 whole bars = 3 × 5 = 15 pieces. Add 2 more pieces: 15 + 2 = 17 pieces. So 3 25 = 175.

items.q: Alfie scores 710 in a spelling test. Maya scores 1620. Who did better?
items.e: Use twentieths: 710 = 1420. 16 is more than 14, so Maya did better.

items.q: Ethan has a plank of wood 94 m long. He says it is longer than 2 m. Is he right?
c: Yes. 94 m = 2 14 m
No. 94 m = 1 14 m
No. 94 m = 49 m
items.e: 4 quarters make 1 m, so 8 quarters make 2 m. 9 − 8 = 1 quarter is left over. So 94 m = 2 14 m, which is longer than 2 m.
